title: Copy Old Pathways, Mostly at the Top

scenes.visual: Dark slate background with slow drifting particles. Clean white title card centered: 'Copy Old Pathways, Mostly at the Top'. Below it sits a small schematic preview of our carried colour map: a teal receptor block across a thin cell membrane above a coral core circle.

scenes.tts: Human genes encode five hundred eighteen protein kinases, including fifty eight receptor tyrosine kinases. Baker's yeast has roughly one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty kinases, and none of those receptors. So where did ours come from?
scenes.caption: Human genes encode 518 protein kinases, including 58 receptor tyrosine kinases. Baker's yeast has roughly 120 to 130 kinases, and none of those receptors. So where did ours come from?
scenes.visual: Schematic side-by-side genome counters fill 70 percent of frame height. Left: 'Baker's yeast' gauge rises smoothly to '120–130 kinases' with a flat zero slot labelled '0 RTKs'. Right: 'Human' gauge rises smoothly to '518 kinases' with a glowing teal band labelled '58 RTKs'. Ambient counter pulses keep motion alive.
scenes.narration: Human genes encode 518 protein kinases, including 58 receptor tyrosine kinases. Baker's yeast has roughly 120 to 130 kinases, and none of those receptors. So where did ours come from?

scenes.tts: You might expect humans to have invented dozens of new signaling pathways. Genomes show the opposite. Fruit flies and humans share the same short list of eight core animal pathways. What changed on the way to vertebrates was how many copies each layer holds.
scenes.caption: You might expect humans to have invented dozens of new signaling pathways. Genomes show the opposite. Fruit flies and humans share the same short list of eight core animal pathways. What changed on the way to vertebrates was how many copies each layer holds.
scenes.visual: The counters morph into a carried two-layer cell schematic: a membrane strip along the top and a compact cytoplasm below. Eight labelled pathway icons (GPCR, Nuclear, TGF-beta, Notch, JAK-STAT, Hedgehog, Wnt, RTK) glow identically on a 'Fly' cell and a 'Human' cell; on the human cell, teal receptor blocks at the top multiply while the eight pathway slots stay the same.
scenes.narration: You might expect humans to have invented dozens of new signaling pathways. Genomes show the opposite. Fruit flies and humans share the same short list of eight core animal pathways. What changed on the way to vertebrates was how many copies each layer holds.

scenes.tts: Compare humans with four invertebrates, adjusting for gene number. Each ratio is a family's share of human genes, divided by its share of invertebrate genes. One means growth in step with genes. All protein kinases score one point two. M A P kinases score one point eight. E G F receptors, two point five. Receptor tyrosine kinases, two point nine.
scenes.caption: Compare humans with four invertebrates, adjusting for gene number. Each ratio is a family's share of human genes, divided by its share of invertebrate genes. One means growth in step with genes. All protein kinases score 1.2. MAP kinases score 1.8. EGF receptors, 2.5. Receptor tyrosine kinases, 2.9.
scenes.visual: Computed horizontal bar chart (labelled 'Human vs. 4 invertebrates, gene-adjusted — Amit et al., 2007') grows left to right beside the cell schematic, under a formula line 'ratio = (family ÷ all genes, human) ÷ (family ÷ all genes, invertebrates)' shown as the ratio is defined, with a vertical dashed reference line at 1.0x. Bars animate in as spoken: slate 'All kinases: 1.2x', coral 'MAP kinases: 1.8x', amber 'EGF receptors: 2.5x', teal 'All RTKs: 2.9x'. The teal receptor layer on the cell swells visibly more than the coral core below.
scenes.narration: Compare humans with four invertebrates, adjusting for gene number. Each ratio is a family's share of human genes, divided by its share of invertebrate genes. One means growth in step with genes. All protein kinases score 1.2. MAP kinases score 1.8. EGF receptors, 2.5. Receptor tyrosine kinases, 2.9.

scenes.tts: Where did the extra receptors come from? Copying errors duplicate single genes, or sometimes whole genomes. Early jawed vertebrates went through two whole genome doublings. One E G F receptor times two makes two, and two times two makes four. That is the likely route from one receptor, as in flies, to four in humans.
scenes.caption: Where did the extra receptors come from? Copying errors duplicate single genes, or sometimes whole-genomes. Early jawed vertebrates went through two whole-genome doublings. One EGF receptor times two makes two, and two times two makes four. That is the likely route from one receptor, as in flies, to four in humans.
scenes.visual: Schematic on the carried cell membrane. A single teal receptor block labelled '1' splits smoothly into two ('1 × 2 = 2'), then each splits again into four ('2 × 2 = 4'). Below the membrane, live labels track 'Fly: 1 EGF receptor' transforming into 'Human: 4 EGF receptors', with a small note 'likely route'. Particles drift continuously along the membrane.
scenes.narration: Where did the extra receptors come from? Copying errors duplicate single genes, or sometimes whole-genomes. Early jawed vertebrates went through two whole-genome doublings. One EGF receptor times two makes two, and two times two makes four. That is the likely route from one receptor, as in flies, to four in humans.

scenes.tts: Once a gene is copied, the original keeps working, so the spare is free to change. Most spares decay into pseudogenes, copies that make no working protein. Or the copies divide the old job. Say the old receptor worked in gut and nerve. One copy loses the D N A that turns it on in gut, the other the nerve D N A. Now both must stay.
scenes.caption: Once a gene is copied, the original keeps working, so the spare is free to change. Most spares decay into pseudogenes, copies that make no working protein. Or the copies divide the old job. Say the old receptor worked in gut and nerve. One copy loses the DNA that turns it on in gut, the other the nerve DNA. Now both must stay.
scenes.visual: Schematic zooms onto two teal receptor copies on the membrane. First branch: the spare acquires a jagged crack, dims to slate grey, and fades down labelled 'Pseudogene (lost)'. Second branch: two copies each start with two bright tissue tags, 'Gut' and 'Nerve'; left loses 'Nerve', right loses 'Gut', and a bracket locks both active copies in place labelled 'Job split'.
scenes.narration: Once a gene is copied, the original keeps working, so the spare is free to change. Most spares decay into pseudogenes, copies that make no working protein. Or the copies divide the old job. Say the old receptor worked in gut and nerve. One copy loses the DNA that turns it on in gut, the other the nerve DNA. Now both must stay.

scenes.tts: A third, rarer outcome: one copy evolves a new job, like binding a different signal. One ancestral receptor becomes a family of relatives listening to different outside messages. But more receptors raise a wiring puzzle.
scenes.caption: A third, rarer outcome: one copy evolves a new job, like binding a different signal. One ancestral receptor becomes a family of relatives listening to different outside messages. But more receptors raise a wiring puzzle.
scenes.visual: Schematic on the same membrane: a spare teal receptor's outer pocket reshapes and shifts to amber, catching a new triangular amber ligand while the original teal receptor keeps catching its round teal ligand. Four distinct teal and amber receptors now sit across the membrane above an empty space waiting to be wired.
scenes.narration: A third, rarer outcome: one copy evolves a new job, like binding a different signal. One ancestral receptor becomes a family of relatives listening to different outside messages. But more receptors raise a wiring puzzle.

scenes.tts: Suppose one pathway has one receptor over a three kinase core, four genes in all. Four separate pathways would take four times four, or sixteen genes. Four receptors sharing one core take four plus three, just seven genes. Looking at our genome bars, which layout fits better?
scenes.caption: Suppose one pathway has one receptor over a three-kinase core, four genes in all. Four separate pathways would take four times four, or sixteen genes. Four receptors sharing one core take four plus three, just seven genes. Looking at our genome bars, which layout fits better?
scenes.visual: Schematic splits the frame below the four membrane receptors. Left: '4 separate tracks' drops four vertical chains of three coral kinases each, tallying '4 × 4 = 16 genes' as spoken. Right: 'Shared core' funnels all four receptors into one stack of three coral kinases, tallying '4 + 3 = 7 genes'. Top corner pins the compact 'RTKs 2.9x vs. MAPKs 1.8x' bars.
scenes.narration: Suppose one pathway has one receptor over a three-kinase core, four genes in all. Four separate pathways would take four times four, or sixteen genes. Four receptors sharing one core take four plus three, just seven genes. Looking at our genome bars, which layout fits better?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic split ('4 separate tracks: 16 genes' vs. 'Shared core: 7 genes') with the compact 'RTKs 2.9x vs. MAPKs 1.8x' bars pinned above. A high-contrast question card pulses gently at center bottom: 'Which layout fits the genome bars better?' Slow ambient shimmer keeps the frame alive during the pause.

scenes.tts: A shared core fits better, because receptors multiplied faster than the kinases below them. Separate tracks would grow both layers equally. Receptors funnel into a few heavily connected proteins called hubs, such as Ras. The core grew modestly too, and gene counts cannot prove wiring. Even so, animal signaling expanded by copying old pathways, mostly at the receptor end.
scenes.caption: A shared core fits better, because receptors multiplied faster than the kinases below them. Separate tracks would grow both layers equally. scenes.visual: The left 16-gene layout dims smoothly (never labelled 'rejected') while the right shared-core schematic expands to center stage. Glowing lines connect all four teal and amber receptors into a prominent coral hub labelled 'Ras', which expands modestly from one node to three smaller linked circles as the caveat is spoken, with a subtle note 'Counts alone do not prove wiring'.
scenes.narration: A shared core fits better, because receptors multiplied faster than the kinases below them. Separate tracks would grow both layers equally. Receptors funnel into a few heavily connected proteins called hubs, such as Ras. The core grew modestly too, and gene counts cannot prove wiring. Even so, animal signaling expanded by copying old pathways, mostly at the receptor end.

scenes.visual: Clean end card on dark slate with slow drifting particles, displaying one single line of large crisp white text centered: 'Animal signaling expanded by copying old pathways, mostly at the receptor end.' No second line, no subtitle.
